item.title: Can Israel’s Opposition Unseat Netanyahu?
item.description:
More than two weeks after one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, there is still uncertainty about who will lead the country.

The spotlight has fallen on the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to make all kinds of deals to build a coalition that could run the government.

David Halbfinger, The New York Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, explains the compromises that Mr. Eisenkot will need to make, and what will happen if he can’t.

Guest: David M. Halbfinger, the Jerusalem bureau chief for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli tasked with forming a government?
  • Here’s how Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Photo: Amir Levy/Getty Images

item.title: What Jensen Huang’s Resignation Will Mean for A.I.
item.description:
This episode was recorded before the news of Mr. Huang’s resignation was made public.

Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that he had extramarital relationships with a woman identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese spy and an executive at the company. In a memo this week, Mr. Huang admitted to being “unfaithful” to his wife.

Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The Times, discusses how everything unraveled for Mr. Huang and what his exit could mean for his and Nvidia’s future.

Guest: Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia after news of his affairs was made public.
  • Nvidia shares plunged, shaking up tech stocks as Mr. Huang stepped down from his role.

Photo: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times

item.title: Public Schools Have a New Crisis: Not Enough Students
item.description:
The number of students in America’s public schools is shrinking. In some cases, the declines have been so drastic that districts are facing empty classrooms, painful budget cuts and angry debates about whether to close schools.

Sarah Mervosh, an education reporter at The New York Times, discusses what the enrollment crisis looks like, why it’s happening and how one school district hopes to fix it.

Guest: Sarah Mervosh, an education reporter at The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • American schools are facing a crisis as the number of children drops.
  • Why U.S. test scores are in a “generation-long decline.”

item.title: Secrets, Chips and Spycraft: The Nvidia C.E.O. Scandal
item.description:
Over the weekend, Jensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of Nvidia — which makes the chips that power artificial intelligence — admitted to having an affair with a woman who has been determined by U.S. officials to be a spy. That revelation came after The New York Times broke the story of how U.S. intelligence officers uncovered what they say was a plot by Alice Huang to use their relationship to funnel information to Beijing.

Tripp Mickle, a White House correspondent for The Times, explains how Beijing tried to compromise one of the tech executives closest to President Trump, and what the scandal could mean for a company with enormous influence over the future of A.I. — and the entire American economy.

Guest: Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Jensen Huang’s tight grip on Nvidia presents a challenge for the company’s board, which is investigating his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
  • Mr. Huang acknowledged having had a relationship with a business executive who U.S. officials determined was working for Chinese intelligence.

Photo: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

item.title: After a Crushing Defeat, Trump Doubles Down

item.title: Chuck Schumer on Governing With (Or Without) Trump
item.description:
Warning: This episode contains strong language.

Last spring, the political picture for Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, was downright bleak. President Trump was back in the White House. Schumer’s Democratic caucus was largely powerless to stop him. And restless Democratic activists were calling for Schumer to resign.

Fast forward to this week. Democrats have roared back to power in both the Senate, where the party flipped seven Republican seats, and the House. And now Schumer, who personally recruited several of the winning candidates, is poised to become the next Senate majority leader with an unambiguous goal: reining in Trump.

On Thursday afternoon, I visited Schumer’s office in the U.S. Capitol to talk about all of that during a 45-minute interview. In between profanity-laced descriptions of the president, Schumer laid out his plans for Senate Democrats over the next two years, including investigations into the Trump administration and legislation seeking to lower Americans’ cost of living.

Guest: Chuck Schumer, the Senate Minority leader.

Last spring, the political picture for Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, was downright bleak. President Trump was back in the White House. Schumer’s Democratic caucus was largely powerless to stop him. And restless Democratic activists were calling for Schumer to resign.
Fast forward to this week. Democrats have roared back to power in both the Senate, where the party flipped seven Republican seats, and the House. And now Schumer, who personally recruited several of the winning candidates, is poised to become the next Senate majority leader with an unambiguous goal: reining in Trump.
On Thursday afternoon, I visited Schumer’s office in the U.S. Capitol to talk about all of that during a 45-minute interview. In between profanity-laced descriptions of the president, Schumer laid out his plans for Senate Democrats over the next two years, including investigations into the Trump administration and legislation seeking to lower Americans’ cost of living.

item.title: The Battle Over Black Representation in the South
item.description:
The approach to this year’s midterms has brought two hugely consequential changes to voting for Black Americans: the gutting of the Voting Rights Act, and redistricting. In the wake of those actions, efforts are underway to mobilize Black voters in the South.

In Mississippi, the Senate battle is being seen as a sleeper race, and the Black Democrat running has a chance of flipping the seat, but state lawmakers are trying to redraw the maps and do away with their one majority Black district.

Today, Emily Cochrane, a reporter covering the American South for The New York Times, addresses the implications for voters across the region — not just in the midterms, but for years to come.

Guest: Emily Cochrane, a national reporter for The New York Times covering the American South.

Background reading: 

  • Black Democratic candidates running in the South have implored Black voters to go to the polls in response to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act.
  • High-profile Democrats across the country have some hope in Scott Colom’s bid for a seat in the Senate.

item.title: James Talarico on the Rage Economy, Billionaires and Flipping Texas
item.description:
James Talarico is asking Texas to do something it hasn’t done in nearly 40 years: Elect a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. It won’t be easy. It will take a vast coalition of Democrats, independents and Republicans in a bright red state that President Trump won by about 14 percentage points in 2024 — and where Republicans have plowed hundreds of millions of dollars into beating Mr. Talarico. And yet, poll after poll shows that Mr. Talarico could pull it off and defeat his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and a Trump ally. 

On Monday, nearly two weeks before Election Day, Michael Barbaro spoke with Mr. Talarico about the kind of race he’s running, why it has succeeded so far in appealing to Republicans and what he wants Democrats to do if they flip control of the Senate on Nov. 3.

Guest: James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas.

Background reading: 

  • Top Democrats, who have long been hesitant to spend money in Texas, have started to back Mr. Talarico.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder Keep Us Guessing
item.description:
The comedian Nathan Fielder came to fame as the creator and host of the Comedy Central series “Nathan for You.” The show followed Fielder as he devised outrageous schemes, ostensibly with the aim of helping various small businesses. What became clear, though, was that Fielder was less interested in helping business owners generate profits than he was in understanding the people ensnared in his plots. His next project, the HBO series “The Rehearsal,” was a similar offbeat portrait of offbeat people. At the center of both projects is Fielder himself, a documentarian whose motives can sometimes be hard to parse.

This week, Fielder’s first feature-length documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters. Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, the movie shows Fielder embedding himself into the life of the disgraced Theranos founder and felon Elizabeth Holmes in the days leading up to her imprisonment for fraud. The film caused a big splash when it debuted at the Telluride Film Festival, in part because it presents Holmes, a mysterious and compelling cultural figure, through the eyes of Fielder, a mysterious and compelling filmmaker.

This week, the Times movie critic Alissa Wilkinson and critic at large Jason Zinoman, who covers comedy, join Michael Barbaro for a spoiler-free discussion of Nathan Fielder, his career, and why he might be the perfect person to tell the story of Elizabeth Holmes.

Jason Zinoman, a critic at large for the Culture section of The New York Times.

  • ‘The Real World’ and Nathan Fielder can both thank this cult filmmaker.
  • ‘You Can See Everything,’ if you could only secure a ticket.

item.title: MAGA's Midterm Defectors
item.description:
Perhaps no American feels the domestic effects of the war, tariffs and inflation more than the Iowa farmer. The political environment stirred up by those farmers’ strife could allow the Democrats to seize the moment and elect one of theirs to the Senate or the governor’s mansion for the first time in 20 years — making Iowa potentially one of the most important states on the map this midterm cycle.

Today, we follow Caleb Renner, a young farmer in north central Iowa, as he shows the effects of the past two years on his community and talks about why those effects may lead him to turn on the Republican Party for the first time, and whether that will translate into support for Democrats.

Guest: Caleb Renner, a farmer in Klemme, Iowa.

Background reading: 

  • Who’s winning the race for Congress?
  • ‘Survival Mode Time’: Republicans accelerate their break with Trump.

item.title: The Republican Strategy to Salvage the Midterms
item.description:
With Republicans trailing in the polls, the party is making hard choices about where to spend its money — abandoning some races while pouring resources into others.

Shane Goldmacher, Nate Cohn and Lisa Lerer, political correspondents for The New York Times, explain why President Trump is campaigning almost daily in deep-red territory, how his influence is shaping the strategy and whether Democrats can win over the disenchanted voters they may need to take back the House and the Senate.

Guests: 

  • Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.
  • Lisa Lerer, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Economic pain and an unpopular Trump have put the G.O.P. on its heels.
  • Top Republican groups are pulling support from two House incumbents.

Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
